title: The god, the demon and the pan of water
hookLine: a god and a demon study for thirty-two years, are told to look in a pan of water, and both walk away thinking the reflection is the self
last: DAHARA — BRAHMAN DWELLS IN BRAHMAN DWELLS IN THE SPACE IN THE HEART.

lines: WE POINT AT PICTURES AND SAY ME.
cards: A mirror by the front door. Good shirt. Hair right.
That's me, says the glance, before any thought. Then a selfie: me again. Then a tagged photo from ten years ago: somehow, also me.
People point at a lot of pictures and say me. The Chandogya tells of two students who did exactly that, and one of them took the mistake home and built a whole philosophy on it.

teach.h: A SELF FREE FROM DEATH AND GRIEF.
teach.b: Prajapati, the lord of creatures, announces: there is a self free from evil, from old age and death, from grief, hunger and thirst. Whoever finds it gains all worlds. The gods and the demons both hear.
The gods send their king, Indra. The demons send theirs, Virochana.

The two rivals arrive with firewood in their hands, not speaking to each other, and live as students for thirty-two years. Then Prajapati teaches: the person seen in the eye, that is the self. Immortal, fearless.
That is Brahman. They ask: and the one seen in water, or in a mirror? It's seen in all these, he says.

teach.h: LOOK IN A PAN OF WATER.
teach.b: Look at yourselves in a pan of water. What do you see? Our whole selves, sir, down to the hair and the nails.
Now dress up well, put on ornaments, and look again. Just as we are, sir, well dressed and adorned, so are these two. That is the self, says Prajapati, immortal, fearless.

Both leave content. Prajapati watches them go: they go without having found the self. Shankara and other commentators say he meant the seer behind the eye, and the students heard the image in the eye.
Virochana goes home and teaches the demons that the body is the self: honor it, adorn it, serve it. Indra sets off too, but on the road, something starts to bother him.
Hindu teachers call Virochana's the first and easiest mistake about the self: taking the body for the atman.
This week, from the top: satya, standing on what's real. Narada, a knower of words. The ladder inward, and food honored as Brahman.
The infinite. Brahman in the heart.
And today, the reflection mistaken for the one who sees.

how: Vedanta teachers often use the story of Indra and Virochana to introduce the difference between the body and the self, and the story's stages are read as a step-by-step inquiry into who we are.

o: the king of the demons, Indra's rival student
lord of creatures, who teaches Indra and Virochana
the king of the gods who goes back to learn more

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: where they look for the self

s: Indra and Virochana came together as friends
they came separately, not speaking to each other, rivals.
Prajapati says they go without having found the self
he watches them leave, satisfied with the reflection.
Virochana teaches the demons that the body is the self
he goes home content and teaches them to honor and adorn the body.

games.q: you're Indra. you've seen yourself, well dressed and adorned, in a pan of water, and Prajapati has said: that is the self. what do you do?
o: set off, but begin to have doubts on the road.
games.why: Virochana goes home satisfied. Indra sets off too, but something starts to bother him, and tomorrow he comes back.

practice: Picture your face in a mirror, clearly, and then ask gently: who's looking?
Don't answer with words; turn your attention back toward the looking itself, like turning around in a doorway, and each time you drift back to the picture, turn around again.

wordCard.voice: Prajapati, lord of creatures. A god and a demon look in a pan of water, adorned, and both mistake the reflection for the self Prajapati described.

orig.note: Sanskrit prajāpati: lord of creatures, the creator figure who teaches Indra and Virochana.

carryVoice: Your line: the reflection isn't you. On the road, Indra isn't so sure. Week four of year two, done.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7.1–4 (Prajapati's proclamation; Indra and Virochana; thirty-two years; the person in the eye)
Chandogya Upanishad 8.8.1–5 (the pan of water; adorned; Virochana's teaching)
